basic-w1-0.title: Find your why
basic-w1-0.idea: A topic names what is in the video; purpose names the change you want in the viewer. The same place can inform, persuade, evoke a feeling, document or entertain. A purpose line connects one viewer to one intended takeaway. Keep your first clip as an honest baseline, before trying to improve it.
basic-w1-0.example: Name a viewer and what you want them to understand, feel or do. Write three purposes with different shot choices, not just different topics. Describe one observable strength and one gap in your unpolished baseline.
steps: Record a 30-second baseline of a familiar subject. Answer: who is it for, what should they take away, and why would they care? Write three different purpose lines and five possible shots for each. Save your text and, if available, one still.
minimum: Name a viewer and what you want them to understand, feel or do.
Write three purposes with different shot choices, not just different topics.
Describe one observable strength and one gap in your unpolished baseline.
basic-w1-0.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w1-1.title: Know your viewer
basic-w1-1.idea: A useful viewer is a real person in a real viewing situation. Someone scrolling without sound needs an opening they can read visually. Someone unfamiliar with your setting may need more context. Ask one person what they notice before explaining your intention.
basic-w1-1.example: Identify one specific viewer and their need. Connect sound, screen or viewing situation to your opening shot. Record one viewer response and a resulting change to your purpose.
steps: Create a Viewer Card: person, need, viewing place, sound on or off, and first-shot idea. Interview one possible viewer. Revise your purpose line using what you heard.
minimum: Identify one specific viewer and their need.
Connect sound, screen or viewing situation to your opening shot.
Record one viewer response and a resulting change to your purpose.
basic-w1-1.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w1-2.title: Learn to see
basic-w1-2.idea: Observation comes before camera technique. “A busy street” is general; “a hand pauses before passing a warm cup” is specific. Look for light, detail, behaviour, contrast and change. A detail earns its place when you can explain what it tells this viewer.
basic-w1-2.example: Include at least five concrete details among 15 observations. Give a viewer-related reason for three observations. Notice light, detail, behaviour, contrast and change.
steps: Take a silent 10-minute walk. Record 15 observations in your Noticing Journal, with at least five specific details. Choose three and explain why each matters to your purpose.
minimum: Include at least five concrete details among 15 observations.
Give a viewer-related reason for three observations.
Notice light, detail, behaviour, contrast and change.
basic-w1-2.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w1-3.title: Choose your shots
basic-w1-3.idea: A place shot gives context, an action or person shot shows what happens, and a detail directs attention. Hold shots long enough to give an editor choices. Write “This shot exists to…” before filming, then compare your reason with what a viewer actually sees.
basic-w1-3.example: Give a purpose-linked reason for each of six shots. Include two shots per category with 10-second holds. Record a viewer guess and compare it with your intention.
steps: Capture six shots: two of place, two of person or action, and two details. Hold each for at least 10 seconds. Add a reason for every shot to the Shot Reasoning Log. Ask a stand-in viewer to guess your purpose.
minimum: Give a purpose-linked reason for each of six shots.
Include two shots per category with 10-second holds.
Record a viewer guess and compare it with your intention.
basic-w1-3.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w1-4.title: Purpose and Seeing: make a comparison
basic-w1-4.idea: Ordering the same place differently changes its meaning. Compare the sequence with your purpose rather than adding effects. Viewer responses are evidence, including disagreement. Return to your baseline and name a specific decision you now make differently.
basic-w1-4.example: Make two six-shot sequences with genuinely different purposes. Record two viewers’ responses without rewriting them as praise. Name a specific change from your original baseline.
steps: Show one place in two different ways: two purposes, six shots each and 12 reasoning-log lines. Ask two viewers what each sequence communicates. Compare the result with your baseline and save a weekly reflection.
minimum: Make two six-shot sequences with genuinely different purposes.
Record two viewers’ responses without rewriting them as praise.
Name a specific change from your original baseline.
basic-w1-4.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w2-0.title: Auto-mode truth and set-up
basic-w2-0.idea: Auto mode makes decisions for you, sometimes changing brightness or focus mid-shot. Resolution, orientation and frame rate should fit the intended screen. Artificial lights can flicker at incompatible shutter settings. Learn the controls you actually have; unsupported settings can be described rather than purchased.
basic-w2-0.example: List your device and its available controls, including limitations. Check lens, storage, battery, focus, exposure, sound and a test playback. Connect your resolution, frame rate and orientation to a viewing destination.
steps: Record three auto-mode clips and note what looks right or wrong. Make a Camera Card listing supported resolution, frame rates, orientation, focus and exposure controls. Run a pre-flight check and test for flicker.
minimum: List your device and its available controls, including limitations.
Check lens, storage, battery, focus, exposure, sound and a test playback.
Connect your resolution, frame rate and orientation to a viewing destination.
basic-w2-0.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w2-1.title: Exposure
basic-w2-1.idea: Exposure describes recorded brightness. Shutter time, aperture where available, and ISO or exposure compensation affect it in different ways. Very bright highlights and deep shadows may lose detail. Compare controlled tests of one scene so your choice is about purpose, not simply the brightest image.
basic-w2-1.example: Compare five exposure levels or clearly labelled planned equivalents. Point to an area with lost highlight or shadow detail. Explain why the chosen brightness serves your intended feeling or information.
steps: Make an exposure ladder of one scene at −2, −1, 0, +1 and +2 EV where supported. Identify lost highlight or shadow detail. Choose a version for your purpose and record why.
minimum: Compare five exposure levels or clearly labelled planned equivalents.
Point to an area with lost highlight or shadow detail.
Explain why the chosen brightness serves your intended feeling or information.
basic-w2-1.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w2-2.title: Motion feel
basic-w2-2.idea: Frame rate is the number of frames captured each second; shutter time controls blur within a frame. A shutter near twice the frame rate is a common starting point, not a creative law. Faster shutters can feel crisp or jittery; slower ones smear movement. Keep the action constant when comparing.
basic-w2-2.example: Record six tests or label unsupported settings as planned comparisons. Describe visible motion differences rather than “good” or “bad”. Explain a usable frame-rate and shutter choice in your own words.
steps: Pour water or film a similar action. Compare three frame-rate choices and three shutter choices, where supported, for six tests. Build a “how it feels” table and write your own rule of thumb.
checks: Rule of thumb in own words
minimum: Record six tests or label unsupported settings as planned comparisons.
Describe visible motion differences rather than “good” or “bad”.
Explain a usable frame-rate and shutter choice in your own words.
basic-w2-2.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w2-3.title: Colour and focus
basic-w2-3.idea: White balance changes how neutral objects appear under different light sources. Auto white balance may shift within a shot. Focus lock can prevent hunting, but a moving subject may leave the sharp area. Judge the intended subject rather than assuming that one fixed setting fits every shot.
basic-w2-3.example: Compare auto and set white balance under two lights. Identify at least three sharp takes out of five, or specify a focus test in the alternative. Link one observed problem to a plausible adjustment.
steps: Compare automatic and set white balance in two light conditions. Try five takes of a subject moving toward the camera, aiming for at least three sharp takes. Describe one failure and its fix.
minimum: Compare auto and set white balance under two lights.
Identify at least three sharp takes out of five, or specify a focus test in the alternative.
Link one observed problem to a plausible adjustment.
basic-w2-3.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w2-4.title: Camera and Exposure: make a comparison
basic-w2-4.idea: A settings log is useful when it connects controls to visible results. Compare your deliberate settings with the auto-mode baseline. The aim is repeatable exposure, colour and focus that support a purpose. Ask viewers what changes they notice before describing your choices.
basic-w2-4.example: Record settings and a reason for each of nine shots. Describe exposure, colour and focus control across the three conditions. Compare to auto mode and include two viewer responses.
steps: Capture one scene in three conditions, making nine shots in total. Save settings and reasons, compare with auto mode, and ask two viewers what changed. Save your weekly study.
minimum: Record settings and a reason for each of nine shots.
Describe exposure, colour and focus control across the three conditions.
Compare to auto mode and include two viewer responses.
basic-w2-4.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w3-0.title: Frame as a decision
basic-w3-0.idea: A frame selects information. Wide views explain a place; closer views can emphasise action, expression or texture. Size alone does not create meaning: the chosen information must serve the viewer. Consider what falls outside the frame as deliberately as what stays in it.
basic-w3-0.example: Use six framings with visibly different shot sizes. Explain an inclusion and exclusion for each. Describe what each framing helps a viewer understand or feel.
steps: Make six framings of one person or stand-in object. Label shot size, what you include, what you exclude and what each framing means.
minimum: Use six framings with visibly different shot sizes.
Explain an inclusion and exclusion for each.
Describe what each framing helps a viewer understand or feel.
basic-w3-0.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w3-1.title: Place the subject
basic-w3-1.idea: Thirds, headroom and lead room are tools for directing attention. Give a face room to look or move when that supports the scene. Eyeline affects how connected a viewer feels. Check the edges for accidental crops and choose balance deliberately rather than obeying a grid automatically.
basic-w3-1.example: Show deliberate headroom and space in the direction of action or gaze. Keep eyelines and balance purposeful across five examples. Explain each correction using visible evidence.
steps: Frame five subjects using deliberate headroom, lead room and eyelines. Annotate a correction for each and explain why it helps.
minimum: Show deliberate headroom and space in the direction of action or gaze.
Keep eyelines and balance purposeful across five examples.
Explain each correction using visible evidence.
basic-w3-1.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w3-2.title: Depth and lines
basic-w3-2.idea: Foreground, middle ground and background can separate a subject from its setting. Lines can guide attention or pull it away. A bright object behind a face may dominate even when the framing grid looks correct. Check the background before adding another element.
basic-w3-2.example: Identify foreground, middle ground and background in three shots. Mark a line that directs attention toward something intentional. Identify and correct a distracting background element.
steps: Create three layered shots. Mark foreground, middle ground, background and useful lines. Remove or reframe a distraction and save a comparison.
minimum: Identify foreground, middle ground and background in three shots.
Mark a line that directs attention toward something intentional.
Identify and correct a distracting background element.
basic-w3-2.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w3-3.title: Formats and safe zones
basic-w3-3.idea: A vertical frame may require moving the camera or subject, not merely cropping the sides. Titles and important details need breathing room around interface overlays. Preview the actual destination because safe areas vary. Preserve the purpose when changing format.
basic-w3-3.example: Create three deliberate compositions instead of accidental crops. Keep important detail and titles away from vulnerable edges. Connect each aspect ratio to a viewing situation.
steps: Recompose one idea for 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1. Mark title and subject safe areas. Explain which viewer situation suits each.
minimum: Create three deliberate compositions instead of accidental crops.
Keep important detail and titles away from vulnerable edges.
Connect each aspect ratio to a viewing situation.
basic-w3-3.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w3-4.title: Composition and Shot Sizes: make a comparison
basic-w3-4.idea: A sequence should give new information as shot size changes. Repeating similar frames can feel static even if each is attractive. Use your shot reasoning log to connect variation with purpose, then check the sequence with a viewer.
basic-w3-4.example: Give a purpose-linked reason for all six frames. Use wide, medium, close and detail views meaningfully. Record a viewer response and one resulting improvement.
steps: Create a six-framing sequence that serves your purpose. Keep a reasoning log, show it to a viewer and reflect on one framing decision.
minimum: Give a purpose-linked reason for all six frames.
Use wide, medium, close and detail views meaningfully.
Record a viewer response and one resulting improvement.
basic-w3-4.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w4-0.title: See the light
basic-w4-0.idea: Light has direction and quality. Small apparent sources often create hard-edged shadows; large apparent sources tend to soften them. Time of day changes both direction and colour. Observe the shadow on the subject before deciding whether you need more equipment.
basic-w4-0.example: Mark where light comes from in three observations. Use shadow edges to distinguish hard and soft light. Connect the observed change to time of day.
steps: Make a light map at three times of day. Label direction, hard or soft quality, and the effect on your subject.
minimum: Mark where light comes from in three observations.
Use shadow edges to distinguish hard and soft light.
Connect the observed change to time of day.
basic-w4-0.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w4-1.title: Window light and reflectors
basic-w4-1.idea: Moving around a window changes the balance between bright and shaded areas. A white card bounces some light back without becoming a new powered source. Keep the subject and camera consistent when testing the reflector. Secure the card safely and keep it away from heat.
basic-w4-1.example: Compare front, side and back light on the same subject. Show or describe the shadow change with and without a reflector. Connect a lighting difference to the intended mood.
steps: Try front, side and back light at a window, with and without a white reflector. Compare the face or object and describe the mood.
minimum: Compare front, side and back light on the same subject.
Show or describe the shadow change with and without a reflector.
Connect a lighting difference to the intended mood.
basic-w4-1.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w4-2.title: Mixed light and colour temperature
basic-w4-2.idea: A window and a warm lamp may put different colours on opposite sides of a subject. One white-balance setting cannot always neutralise both. Try switching off a source, moving the subject or embracing a deliberate contrast. Compare before and after in the same framing.
basic-w4-2.example: Identify two differently coloured sources and their effects. Apply one adjustment and describe the improvement or trade-off. Check consistency across the subject and nearby shots.
steps: Combine window light and a warm lamp. Identify the colour problem, then switch off a source or set white balance deliberately. Save a before-and-after explanation.
minimum: Identify two differently coloured sources and their effects.
Apply one adjustment and describe the improvement or trade-off.
Check consistency across the subject and nearby shots.
basic-w4-2.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w4-3.title: Harsh sun and shade
basic-w4-3.idea: Hard overhead sun can create deep eye shadows and bright patches. Moving into open shade or changing the subject’s angle may help more than increasing exposure. A reflector should never dazzle the subject. Protect comfort and permissions before chasing an image.
basic-w4-3.example: Point to a specific harsh-light problem. Make a controlled before-and-after rescue. Check useful detail, shadows and subject comfort.
steps: Rescue a harsh-light setup using shade, repositioning or a reflector. Make a before-and-after study and describe what changed on the face or subject.
minimum: Point to a specific harsh-light problem.
Make a controlled before-and-after rescue.
Check useful detail, shadows and subject comfort.
basic-w4-3.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w4-4.title: Light Basics: make a comparison
basic-w4-4.idea: Good lighting choices serve intent and remain understandable when you explain them. Compare conditions consistently, select rather than collect, and use viewer responses to check whether the intended mood survives.
basic-w4-4.example: Explain how a chosen lighting condition serves the intended mood. Compare four conditions and a controlled rescue. Include a viewer response and one repeatable lesson.
steps: Study one subject in four lighting conditions and make one rescue. State your purpose, collect a viewer response and save your weekly comparison.
minimum: Explain how a chosen lighting condition serves the intended mood.
Compare four conditions and a controlled rescue.
Include a viewer response and one repeatable lesson.
basic-w4-4.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w5-0.title: Listen first
basic-w5-0.idea: Sound communicates space, distance and activity beyond the frame. Listen before recording: a fan, traffic or footsteps may dominate the voice you want. Describe what you actually hear. AI can read your description or a recorder screenshot; it cannot listen to your recording.
basic-w5-0.example: Identify foreground and background sounds. Describe three recognisably different sound environments. Use concrete descriptions of source, distance or change.
steps: Listen to or record 60 seconds in three places. Describe foreground, background and changing sounds. Keep written observations and an optional recorder screenshot.
minimum: Identify foreground and background sounds.
Describe three recognisably different sound environments.
Use concrete descriptions of source, distance or change.
basic-w5-0.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w5-1.title: Mics and placement
basic-w5-1.idea: Distance changes the ratio of direct voice to room reflections and noise. A close phone can outperform an expensive microphone placed too far away. Avoid rubbing clothing or pointing a microphone away from speech. Test before committing to a full interview.
basic-w5-1.example: Document three distances in two rooms. Compare background noise and voice clarity. Choose a setup using the comparison, not the price of the microphone.
steps: Record the same sentence at three distances in two rooms. Compare noise and clarity, then choose a position and explain why. Use text and an optional recorder screenshot.
minimum: Document three distances in two rooms.
Compare background noise and voice clarity.
Choose a setup using the comparison, not the price of the microphone.
basic-w5-1.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w5-2.title: Levels and monitoring
basic-w5-2.idea: A recorder’s level meter shows signal level, not whether a story is clear. Digital clipping can distort loud peaks. Leave headroom; peaks around −12 dBFS are a useful starting target where a meter supports it. Monitor with headphones and adjust to the actual voice.
basic-w5-2.example: Set and describe a level that leaves headroom. Compare three gain levels and identify clipping or its absence. Record what you noticed through headphone monitoring.
steps: Record a sentence at three gain levels. Identify any clipping, set a level with headroom and listen with headphones. Save notes and an optional waveform or meter screenshot.
minimum: Set and describe a level that leaves headroom.
Compare three gain levels and identify clipping or its absence.
Record what you noticed through headphone monitoring.
basic-w5-2.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w5-3.title: Room tone, noise and wind
basic-w5-3.idea: Room tone is the sound of a location when the main action pauses. It can bridge edits without unnatural silence. Wind protection reduces air hitting the microphone, while quieter placement may reduce other noise. Record a comparison rather than assuming a filter solved it.
basic-w5-3.example: Capture or clearly plan consistent room tone for the scene. Compare an unprotected and protected or repositioned recording. Connect the chosen fix to a specific noise source.
steps: Capture room tone and compare wind with and without suitable protection. List practical noise fixes and explain the one you would use.
minimum: Capture or clearly plan consistent room tone for the scene.
Compare an unprotected and protected or repositioned recording.
Connect the chosen fix to a specific noise source.
basic-w5-3.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w5-4.title: Sound: make a comparison
basic-w5-4.idea: Dialogue, ambience and music do different jobs. Keep necessary words intelligible before adding a music bed. The same picture can feel very different with silence, location ambience or music. Use audio you have permission to use and describe the meaning change yourself.
basic-w5-4.example: Describe intelligibility and any remaining speech problems. Use an ambience bed that fits the place without masking speech. Compare the three versions and explain how their meaning changes.
steps: Record a clean sentence and an ambience bed. Compare one clip without sound, with ambience and with permitted music. Write what changes and save a weekly sound study.
minimum: Describe intelligibility and any remaining speech problems.
Use an ambience bed that fits the place without masking speech.
Compare the three versions and explain how their meaning changes.
basic-w5-4.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w6-0.title: Steady the camera
basic-w6-0.idea: Stability starts with stance, support and controlled breathing. A tripod is useful but a safe stable surface or braced elbows can also help. Leave a still moment before and after the action. Judge improvement against your own first hold.
basic-w6-0.example: Complete ten holds and compare their steadiness. Describe stance, support or another repeatable technique. Identify a visible improvement from first to last.
steps: Record ten handheld holds of ten seconds. Rate their steadiness, describe your setup and note what improved. Add a setup photo if available.
minimum: Complete ten holds and compare their steadiness.
Describe stance, support or another repeatable technique.
Identify a visible improvement from first to last.
basic-w6-0.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w6-1.title: Pans and tilts
basic-w6-1.idea: A pan turns horizontally; a tilt moves vertically. Movement is easier to follow when it reveals something or follows an action. Start and end on useful frames and hold them briefly, giving an editor room to cut. A static shot is a valid choice when movement adds nothing.
basic-w6-1.example: Keep the three moves controlled enough to follow. Explain what each movement reveals or follows. Include usable still moments at both ends.
steps: Create three motivated pans or tilts. State the reason for each move and include steady start and end holds.
minimum: Keep the three moves controlled enough to follow.
Explain what each movement reveals or follows.
Include usable still moments at both ends.
basic-w6-1.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w6-2.title: Coverage
basic-w6-2.idea: Coverage supplies the pieces needed to explain an action in an edit. Wide views establish space; closer views show action and detail. A cutaway can bridge a missing moment, but unrelated decoration may confuse the sequence. Anticipate what the editor will need.
basic-w6-2.example: Include the views needed to understand beginning, action and end. Choose a cutaway that can bridge or clarify a moment. Use varied sizes with distinct information.
steps: Film a familiar routine with establishing, wide, medium, detail and cutaway views. Complete a Coverage Checklist and explain why each shot is useful.
minimum: Include the views needed to understand beginning, action and end.
Choose a cutaway that can bridge or clarify a moment.
Use varied sizes with distinct information.
basic-w6-2.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w6-3.title: Continuity
basic-w6-3.idea: Consistent screen direction and eyelines help viewers understand where people are. Draw the line between subjects and plan camera positions deliberately. Matching the point of an action across cuts can hide a transition. The aim is readable geography, not a rule for its own sake.
basic-w6-3.example: Keep directions understandable using a position diagram. Make the participants’ eyelines connect plausibly. Compare the same action across two shots.
steps: Plan or film a two-person conversation using consenting participants or stand-ins. Diagram camera positions and eyelines. Compare screen direction and one matched action.
minimum: Keep directions understandable using a position diagram.
Make the participants’ eyelines connect plausibly.
Compare the same action across two shots.
basic-w6-3.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w6-4.title: Stability, Movement and Coverage: make a comparison
basic-w6-4.idea: An editor should be able to assemble an understandable process from the shots you captured. A missing step is a coverage problem; a repeated explanation may be an editing problem. Test the sequence without narrating over the viewer’s uncertainty.
basic-w6-4.example: Assemble eight to twelve shots into a readable process. Identify usable coverage and any missing or repeated moment. Record a viewer response and one improvement.
steps: Capture and assemble an eight-to-twelve-shot process film. Ask a viewer to describe what happened. Save the coverage checklist, one still and your weekly reflection.
minimum: Assemble eight to twelve shots into a readable process.
Identify usable coverage and any missing or repeated moment.
Record a viewer response and one improvement.
basic-w6-4.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w7-0.title: Organise and ingest
basic-w7-0.idea: A predictable folder structure saves time and protects originals. Keep source media, project files and exports distinct, with names that help you find takes. A backup needs another location, not just another folder on the same failing device. Check that copied files open before deleting anything.
basic-w7-0.example: Separate source media, projects and exports clearly. Use a repeatable name pattern for your examples. Describe an independent backup location and a check that files open.
steps: Organise your footage, project and exports. Set a naming pattern and a backup plan. Save a screenshot or a written folder tree.
minimum: Separate source media, projects and exports clearly.
Use a repeatable name pattern for your examples.
Describe an independent backup location and a check that files open.

basic-w7-1.title: Rough cut
basic-w7-1.idea: A rough cut tests order and meaning before polish. Use the week-six coverage to show the action clearly, remove duplicates and note missing moments. Cutting on action can connect angles; accidental black frames or direction changes may interrupt understanding.
basic-w7-1.example: Give a reason for each main cut. Check movement and action remain understandable. Finish a viewable beginning, middle and end.
steps: Assemble the week-six process footage into a rough cut. Keep a cut log explaining why each change of shot belongs. Check continuity and the ending.

Finish a viewable beginning, middle and end.
basic-w7-1.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w7-2.title: Pace and sound
basic-w7-2.idea: Pacing depends on how long viewers need to understand or feel something. In a J-cut the next audio starts before its picture; in an L-cut the previous audio continues under the new picture. Use those overlaps to connect meaning while keeping speech clear above ambience or music.
basic-w7-2.example: Explain and revise at least one too-long or too-short moment. Keep important speech understandable over other sound. Use or clearly diagram a motivated audio overlap.
steps: Revise the pace of your rough cut, add a deliberate J- or L-cut, and balance dialogue with ambience or music. Describe the effect and save a timeline screenshot if available.
minimum: Explain and revise at least one too-long or too-short moment.
Keep important speech understandable over other sound.
Use or clearly diagram a motivated audio overlap.
basic-w7-2.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w7-3.title: Look and titles
basic-w7-3.idea: Basic correction aims for consistent exposure and colour across shots before a dramatic look. Titles must be readable at the actual viewing size and stay on screen long enough to understand. Simple consistent styling can support a film more than many different effects.
basic-w7-3.example: Compare neighbouring shots for exposure and colour continuity. Check title contrast, duration and safe placement on the destination screen. Use a deliberate, consistent visual style.
steps: Match the colour of neighbouring shots and add one readable title. Preview on a phone or intended screen and save a before-and-after note.

Check title contrast, duration and safe placement on the destination screen.

basic-w7-3.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w7-4.title: Editing Fundamentals: make a comparison
basic-w7-4.idea: A shorter cut forces priorities: preserve what carries the purpose and remove repetition. Export settings should fit the destination, but the exported file still needs playback review. Compare image, sound, titles and file behaviour rather than trusting the timeline preview.
basic-w7-4.example: Explain the main decisions in reducing sixty seconds to thirty. Compare three destination exports or clearly specified export plans. Connect retained moments to the film’s purpose.
steps: Recut a 60-second film to 30 seconds. Prepare versions for YouTube, Instagram and WhatsApp using suitable formats. Compare the exports and explain what survived the shorter edit and why.

basic-w7-4.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w8-0.title: Story shape
basic-w8-0.idea: A mini-story has a situation, a change and a result. A list of facts may explain a place without giving viewers a reason to care. A person who wants something provides direction. Try openings that invite a question rather than promising something the film cannot deliver.
basic-w8-0.example: Describe a beginning, change and ending. Connect a person with something they want. Write three meaningfully different openings.
steps: Turn a plain fact about your place into a mini-story. Identify beginning, middle and end, connect a person to a want, and write three possible openings.
minimum: Describe a beginning, change and ending.
Connect a person with something they want.
Write three meaningfully different openings.
basic-w8-0.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w8-1.title: Person, want, obstacle
basic-w8-1.idea: A small obstacle creates movement without manufacturing conflict. Choose someone you can approach respectfully and film with permission. A Viewer Card and purpose line should connect that person’s situation with a stranger’s reason to watch. Avoid making claims about a person that they have not shared.
basic-w8-1.example: Describe a specific want in plain language. Name a credible obstacle without inventing personal facts. Connect the story to a viewer and intended takeaway.
steps: Choose a person or a clearly labelled fictional stand-in. State their want and obstacle, then write your Viewer Card and capstone purpose line.

basic-w8-1.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w8-2.title: Interview and voice-over
basic-w8-2.idea: Open questions invite stories; leading questions may impose your conclusion. Ask permission, keep the setting comfortable and listen before preparing the next question. A short voice-over can connect images but should not repeat everything the viewer already sees.
basic-w8-2.example: Write five questions that invite more than yes or no. Describe consent, comfort and how you listened. Draft a clear voice-over that adds useful information.
steps: Prepare five open interview questions. Conduct a short consensual interview, or role-play it explicitly. Transcribe the best answer and draft a brief voice-over.

Describe consent, comfort and how you listened.

basic-w8-2.alternative: Use stills, a storyboard or a written comparison instead of filming. Describe each planned test and its expected result, label it as a simulation, and apply the same three criteria to that evidence. Do not claim you captured or heard something you only planned.

basic-w8-3.title: Hooks, endings and shoot
basic-w8-3.idea: An opening sets an expectation; an ending should answer or develop it. Plan the capstone around the person, place and purpose rather than collecting attractive but unrelated shots. A Shot Reasoning Log helps you notice missing evidence while you can still film it.
basic-w8-3.example: Create an opening that honestly invites interest in this story. Plan an ending connected to the opening and purpose. Give a purpose-linked reason for each planned or captured shot.

basic-w8-4.title: Capstone and review
basic-w8-4.idea: Your capstone brings intention, camera work, sound and editing together. Compare it with the first baseline using evidence. Ask three viewers where attention dropped and make a focused revision. A self-check completes the beginner journey; an optional mentor demo review is separate and is not a professional credential.
basic-w8-4.example: Tell a readable 60–90 second story with a clear purpose. Explain exposure, sound and editing decisions using your own evidence. Include the required logs, three viewer responses and a baseline comparison.

Explain exposure, sound and editing decisions using your own evidence.
Include the required logs, three viewer responses and a baseline comparison.

intermediate-w1-0.title: Choose your lens
intermediate-w1-0.idea: Focal length changes angle of view; camera position changes perspective. Cropping a wide image can imitate a tighter field of view, but it does not reproduce moving the camera. Compare from one position first, then move to keep the subject the same size. On a phone, avoid assuming every zoom option uses a separate optical lens. Choose the view that supports the relationship between your subject and its surroundings.
intermediate-w1-0.example: A close wide view of a mug exaggerates the near rim; a more distant tight view makes the background feel less separated in scale. The camera move causes the perspective change.
steps: Compare three available focal lengths or crops from a fixed position. Then make two frames with the subject the same size but different camera distances. Label real lens changes and crops separately.
minimum: Show three labelled fields of view from one position.
Explain how moving the camera changes near/far relationships.
Choose a view and explain what it communicates.
intermediate-w1-0.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w1-1.title: Control depth
intermediate-w1-1.idea: Depth of field is the range that appears acceptably sharp. Aperture, focus distance, focal length, sensor format and viewing conditions interact. A wide aperture alone does not guarantee a useful image: a moving subject may leave the sharp zone. Phone portrait blur is computational and may make edge errors. First decide what must remain readable, then test the focus transition you need.
intermediate-w1-1.example: An interview can isolate a face while keeping a recognisable workshop behind it. Maximum blur may remove the context that makes the interview meaningful.
steps: Make deep and shallow-focus versions of one scene. Mark subject and background distances. Repeat a near-to-far focus change three times, or storyboard it with labelled sharp areas.
minimum: Show two versions and label actual optical or simulated blur.
Record three attempts and identify where focus succeeds or fails.
Explain which background information your choice preserves or removes.
intermediate-w1-1.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w1-2.title: Balance motion and light
intermediate-w1-2.idea: Shutter time affects motion blur as well as exposure. If you shorten it to control bright daylight, movement may look more staccato. A compatible neutral-density filter reduces light without changing the intended shutter or aperture, but it may introduce colour casts. Compare actual footage before choosing. Avoid treating a shutter guideline as a rule that overrides flicker tests or creative intent.
intermediate-w1-2.example: For a bright outdoor product pour, faster shutter makes droplets crisp; shade can preserve a softer motion feel without additional equipment.
steps: Film the same movement with two shutter choices and two brightness-control methods available to you. Record exposure, motion appearance and any colour shift. Choose one setup for your scene.
minimum: Compare the same action at two shutter settings or labelled simulations.
Explain how brightness was controlled in each test.
Identify one compromise and justify your final setup.
intermediate-w1-2.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w1-3.title: Keep shots consistent
intermediate-w1-3.idea: Automatic exposure and white balance can change between angles. Locking controls may help, but each new camera position still needs a check. Use a neutral reference, a consistent monitoring view and a short settings log. A waveform helps compare brightness distribution; it does not decide whether the image tells the right story. Check skin or product colour and important highlights before chasing a perfectly flat match.
intermediate-w1-3.example: A white ceramic cup should not turn orange when the camera moves closer. A neutral reference helps separate a lighting change from an automatic white-balance shift.
steps: Capture a wide, medium and close view under the same light. Match exposure and white balance. Save a contact sheet with settings and annotate one correction.
minimum: Show three views with a consistent intended look.
Record the relevant settings and any automatic limitations.
Point to a mismatch and show or describe a controlled correction.
intermediate-w1-3.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w1-4.title: Camera study
intermediate-w1-4.idea: A visual treatment is a set of decisions that work together. Lens choice, focus, motion and brightness should serve one purpose rather than demonstrate every setting. Edit a short sequence, then watch without your notes. If the treatment changes accidentally between shots, find the cause and reshoot or correct the weakest part. Record what you would repeat on a new shoot.
intermediate-w1-4.example: A calm craft film might favour steady frames, deliberate focus and soft motion. A single frantic handheld insert needs a story reason to belong.
steps: Make a 45–60 second scene with six or more shots. Include your lens, focus and exposure choices, a before/after correction and one viewer response. Save the final study and decision log.

Show consistent focus, brightness and colour across the sequence.
Document one revision prompted by a visible problem or viewer response.
intermediate-w1-4.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w2-0.title: Design the light
intermediate-w2-0.idea: Start with the feeling and the apparent source of light. A key establishes direction; fill changes shadow depth; an edge light may separate the subject. These are roles, not a requirement to own three fixtures. A window, white card and darker background can serve similar purposes. Sketch camera, subject and light positions, then test whether the eyes or important product details remain readable.
intermediate-w2-0.example: A window can be the key and a white wall the fill. Turning the subject changes the balance before another light is needed.
steps: Draw two lighting plans for different moods. Build one with available light and a reflector or negative fill. Photograph the setup and the resulting frame.

Show camera, subject and source positions for two plans.
Identify a detail that remains readable in the chosen setup.
intermediate-w2-0.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w2-1.title: Shape contrast
intermediate-w2-1.idea: Moving a source closer changes its apparent size and the relationship between near and far illumination. Bouncing or diffusing light usually costs output. Negative fill removes reflected light rather than adding brightness. Compare one adjustment at a time and watch both the subject and background. Keep lamps ventilated, secure stands and avoid placing improvised materials against hot fixtures.
intermediate-w2-1.example: A black card beside a shiny cup can define its edge by removing a reflection; adding another light may flatten the shape instead.
steps: Compare direct light, bounced light and negative fill on one subject. Keep framing fixed. Annotate shadow edges, background brightness and the version that suits your brief.
minimum: Change one lighting factor at a time across three comparisons.
Describe shadow edge and brightness differences in specific areas.
Choose a version with a purpose-linked reason.
intermediate-w2-1.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w2-2.title: Record clear dialogue
intermediate-w2-2.idea: A close microphone often improves the ratio of voice to room sound more than a more expensive distant microphone. Placement must avoid clothing rustle, plosives and frame intrusion. Monitor a real test with headphones and leave headroom for louder words. Peaks that do not clip still may contain distracting noise. Get consent before recording and agree which parts can be shared.
intermediate-w2-2.example: Moving a phone recorder closer to an interview subject can reduce room echo. A quiet fan may still become obvious during the pauses.
steps: Record the same short paragraph at three microphone distances. Listen with headphones. Choose a position, record room tone and note consent and background noise.
minimum: Compare three distances with the same voice and room.
Name an audible issue and a placement or room adjustment.
Keep a room-tone sample and a clear consent note.
intermediate-w2-2.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w2-3.title: Protect the location take
intermediate-w2-3.idea: Wind, traffic and intermittent machinery make location sound unpredictable. Scout by listening at the time you will record. Wind protection and repositioning can help, but neither fixes every condition. Capture separate room or environment tone and a clear sync cue when sound is recorded separately. Check for drift on longer takes and keep a backup plan that does not depend on repairing everything later.
intermediate-w2-3.example: Moving behind a wall may reduce wind while changing the background. Decide whether that visual compromise is better than losing intelligible speech.
steps: Plan and record a short outdoor or noisy-room test. Compare two positions, capture a sync cue and 20 seconds of environment tone, and write a fallback location or voice-over plan.
minimum: Compare two positions and identify the cleaner result.
Include a sync cue and a separate ambience sample or labelled plan.
Specify a realistic fallback for an unusable take.
intermediate-w2-3.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w2-4.title: Interview study
intermediate-w2-4.idea: A useful interview sequence combines understandable speech with images that support the meaning. Cutaways can conceal an edit, but they should not imply events that did not happen. Maintain room tone across cuts and balance speech before music. Show the subject or a viewer the relevant sequence and record any concern about meaning or permission. Technical polish does not excuse changing what someone meant.
intermediate-w2-4.example: A maker discussing care can be supported by genuine close-ups of the process, rather than unrelated shots that suggest a false event.
steps: Edit a 60–90 second interview or product demonstration. Include a setup image, sound comparison, three meaningful cutaways and one feedback-based revision.
minimum: Keep the intended subject visible and speech understandable.
Use three cutaways that support rather than distort the words.
Record feedback, permission limits and a resulting revision.
intermediate-w2-4.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w3-0.title: Plan useful coverage
intermediate-w3-0.idea: Coverage gives the editor choices about information and emotion. A master can establish the whole action; closer angles reveal details and reactions. The most useful shot is sometimes the missing transition rather than another attractive close-up. Plan an essential version first, then add alternatives. Identify what must remain continuous and which moments can be repeated safely.
intermediate-w3-0.example: Making tea needs the water before the pour and the cup after it. Five close-ups of steam cannot replace the missing action.
steps: Break a simple action into six beats. Make an essential shot list and two optional shots. Mark the visual information each shot contributes and one continuity risk.
minimum: Cover beginning, change and result across six beats.
Give each essential shot a distinct information purpose.
Identify one continuity risk and how you will track it.
intermediate-w3-0.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w3-1.title: Keep screen direction
intermediate-w3-1.idea: The line of action helps the viewer understand where people or movement are in space. Crossing it without a cue can reverse apparent direction. A neutral angle, motivated move or clear re-establishing view may make a change understandable. The goal is orientation, not blind obedience. Track eyelines and entrances as well as the camera positions.
intermediate-w3-1.example: A person walking left-to-right should not suddenly seem to return unless the edit gives us a reason for the reversal.
steps: Diagram two subjects or stand-ins and a line of action. Shoot three consistent angles, then an intentional line crossing with a visual cue. Compare the sequences.
minimum: Mark subjects, eyelines and camera positions.
Show three angles with understandable screen relationships.
Demonstrate or storyboard a cue that makes a line crossing clear.
intermediate-w3-1.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w3-2.title: Move with a reason
intermediate-w3-2.idea: A camera move changes the viewer’s relationship to information. A reveal, approach or retreat should have a starting frame, a destination and a reason. Stabilisation cannot rescue unclear movement or unsafe footing. Rehearse without recording, protect your route and compare with a static option. A locked frame can be more expressive when the action already carries the scene.
intermediate-w3-2.example: A slow move past a doorway can reveal a workshop gradually. Moving merely because a stabiliser is available adds effort without adding meaning.
steps: Make a static, a reveal and an approach version of the same moment. Mark safe start/end positions. Choose the version that gives the viewer the right information at the right time.
minimum: State what each movement reveals or changes.
Show deliberate beginning and ending frames with a safe route.
Compare against the static version before choosing.
intermediate-w3-2.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w3-3.title: Direct a small action
intermediate-w3-3.idea: Give performers playable actions instead of vague emotions. “Check the broken wheel, then decide whether to repair it” offers something observable. Rehearse timing and keep the space consistent between angles. For documentary subjects, do not present staged actions as spontaneous evidence. Use a consented rehearsal or a clearly labelled fictional exercise when practising direction.
intermediate-w3-3.example: “Hide the note before someone enters” produces clear behaviour. “Be mysterious” gives the performer much less to do.
steps: Direct or self-perform a three-beat action. Capture two takes with one changed instruction. Log timing, prop position and the visible difference.
minimum: Write an observable action rather than only an emotion.
