Compare two takes and explain the effect of the instruction.
intermediate-w3-3.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w3-4.title: Scene study
intermediate-w3-4.idea: Editing tests your coverage. First assemble the scene without music or effects and ask whether a viewer can follow the action. Then shape attention with duration, reactions and sound bridges. If a cut confuses, identify whether information, direction or timing is missing. Fix the smallest cause rather than hiding it under a transition.
intermediate-w3-4.example: Holding a reaction longer can change a scene from efficient to hesitant without adding a new shot.
steps: Create a 60–90 second scene from your coverage. Make two pacing versions, get one viewer response, then deliver a final cut with a short continuity and revision log.
minimum: A viewer can describe the action and spatial relationships.
Compare two versions with different meaningful cut timing.
Identify and repair a specific confusing moment.
intermediate-w3-4.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w4-0.title: Build a reliable edit
intermediate-w4-0.idea: Organise media before making creative changes. Preserve original files, use meaningful folders and keep project versions. Proxies can improve playback while retaining a link to the original media. Confirm frame rate, resolution and audio settings at the start. Relink and export a short test before committing a long project to an unfamiliar workflow.
intermediate-w4-0.example: A beautiful edit is difficult to revise if its audio lives in a temporary download folder that disappears the next day.
steps: Organise a small project with originals, audio, graphics, exports and project versions. Build a rough cut and test relinking or reopening it from a saved copy.
minimum: Use a folder and naming structure another person can follow.
Record timeline and delivery settings.
Demonstrate a reopen or relink test without deleting originals.
intermediate-w4-0.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w4-1.title: Refine timing and sound
intermediate-w4-1.idea: J-cuts introduce incoming sound before the picture changes; L-cuts let outgoing sound continue across the next image. Both can connect ideas, but speech meaning must remain intact. Balance dialogue first, then ambience, effects and music. Check on headphones and an ordinary speaker. A louder mix may feel exciting while masking the information the audience needs.
intermediate-w4-1.example: An interview voice can introduce the workshop before the picture cuts there, allowing the viewer to connect place and meaning.
steps: Refine a rough cut with two purposeful sound bridges. Balance speech and background layers, compare on two playback devices and note one revision.
minimum: Explain the purpose of two sound bridges.
Keep essential speech or subject sound readable.
Record observations from two listening conditions.
intermediate-w4-1.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w4-2.title: Match before styling
intermediate-w4-2.idea: Colour correction aims for deliberate consistency; a creative grade establishes a look. Start with exposure and white balance, compare neighbouring shots, then apply restrained style. A LUT is a transform or look, not an automatic repair tool. Check the expected input colour space before using one. Use scopes and the image together, and watch for clipped channels or unnatural product colours.
intermediate-w4-2.example: A warm workshop can remain warm without turning a neutral product unnaturally orange in only one angle.
steps: Match three neighbouring shots, then create two restrained looks. Save before/after stills, record your order of operations and choose a look for the story.
minimum: Show consistent intended brightness and neutral colour across three shots.
Separate corrections from the creative treatment.
Explain a visible reason for choosing one look.
intermediate-w4-2.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w4-3.title: Make accessible exports
intermediate-w4-3.idea: Delivery is a viewing test, not just an export button. Reframe deliberately for a second aspect ratio, check text size on a phone and proofread captions. Captions should convey meaningful speech and relevant sound without covering the subject. Compare the exported file with the timeline for missing media, unexpected colour or sound changes. Requirements vary by destination, so record the actual brief.
intermediate-w4-3.example: Simply cropping a wide interview to vertical can cut off the speaker’s hands and useful objects. Reframing should preserve the reason those details were shown.
steps: Export a landscape and vertical version. Add and proofread captions, inspect the edges and play both files end to end on the intended screen. Keep a delivery checklist.
minimum: Preserve the important action in both aspect ratios.
Proofread captions and check their placement on a phone.
Record an end-to-end playback check and the delivery settings.
intermediate-w4-3.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

intermediate-w4-4.title: Intermediate film
intermediate-w4-4.idea: A complete film should connect its brief, captured material and final edit. Assess what the viewer receives, not how many techniques were used. Compare the result with the first rough cut and identify the strongest improvement. Archive the media, final export and a short decision log so the work can be reopened. This project demonstrates practice, not professional certification.
intermediate-w4-4.example: A small-business film succeeds when a viewer understands the useful difference the product makes, even if the final edit uses simple cuts.
steps: Deliver a 60–120 second film and a second-format cut. Include your brief, six-frame contact sheet, captioned export, viewer response and one documented revision.
minimum: Connect the film’s opening, development and ending to the brief.
Identify evidence of controlled image, sound and editing choices.
Provide both versions and a clear revision and archive note.
intermediate-w4-4.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w1-0.title: Write a creative brief
advanced-w1-0.idea: A creative brief defines the audience, desired response, deliverables and constraints. Separate an assumption from something you have actually learned from the viewer or stakeholder. A precise brief gives you a way to reject attractive ideas that do not serve the job. Define a small, observable success test and protect room for creative exploration within the constraints.
advanced-w1-0.example: A film meant to build trust in a maker requires different evidence from a ten-second announcement of a discount.
steps: Write a one-page brief for a 2–3 minute film. Include audience, change, deliverables, constraints and a viewer test. Record one piece of real feedback or clearly label your assumptions.
minimum: Identify one audience and intended response.
List deliverables, access, time and equipment constraints.
Define a viewer test that can disagree with your intention.
advanced-w1-0.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w1-1.title: Build a visual treatment
advanced-w1-1.idea: A treatment connects references to decisions you can execute. Study contrast, framing, camera distance, movement and pacing rather than copying surface colour alone. Explain what each reference contributes and where your project differs. Keep references attributed; they are study material, not footage you can automatically reuse. Test one image and one edit idea before treating the look as settled.
advanced-w1-1.example: A wide, quiet frame can make a character seem isolated. Copying its teal shadows without the spatial choice may miss the point.
steps: Build a six-frame treatment using your own tests or attributed references. State a framing, lighting and pacing rule. Include one deliberate exception and a practical test.
minimum: Explain the useful decision in each reference.
Write three rules that serve the brief.
Show a test and explain whether an exception improves it.
advanced-w1-1.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w1-2.title: Shape a scene arc
advanced-w1-2.idea: A scene can change information, intention or emotion even when little physical action occurs. Define what the viewer knows at the start and what changes by the end. Beats should cause or complicate the next moment. For factual work, structure must respect what happened and what the evidence supports. A strong ending resolves or reframes the question the film actually raised.
advanced-w1-2.example: A repair story changes when the maker discovers the missing part. That discovery can carry the middle more effectively than a montage of unrelated tools.
steps: Make a beat board for your film with six to ten moments. Label the change in each beat, its supporting shot or sound, and the question the ending answers.
minimum: Describe the viewer’s knowledge or feeling before and after.
Connect beats through cause, contrast or development.
Tie the ending to evidence and the opening question.
advanced-w1-2.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w1-3.title: Plan the production
advanced-w1-3.idea: A workable production plan prioritises essential coverage and identifies dependencies. Group setups sensibly, allow resets and breaks, and plan what happens if access or weather changes. Obtain permission for locations, contributors and assets before filming. A solo plan still needs safety, backups and a clear stopping point. Avoid specialised rigs, electrical work or hazardous locations without qualified support.
advanced-w1-3.example: A two-hour interview booking can disappear into lighting if the setup has never been rehearsed. A short test makes the schedule more realistic.
steps: Create a schedule, shot priorities, equipment list, permission checklist and two fallback plans. Test the longest setup and revise your time estimate.
minimum: Include setup, recording, reset, breaks and data backup time.
Identify permissions and practical risks for the actual location.
Specify two workable alternatives and a tested setup estimate.
advanced-w1-3.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w1-4.title: Treatment test
advanced-w1-4.idea: A proof of concept should test the riskiest creative assumption, not merely the easiest shot. Assemble a short sequence that combines your intended image and sound approach. Ask viewers what they infer without giving the explanation first. Compare their response with the brief, then revise a rule, beat or production assumption before the main shoot.
advanced-w1-4.example: If viewers read a carefully lit room as threatening when you intended warmth, that is useful evidence before the full shoot.
steps: Produce a 20–30 second proof of concept. Test it with two viewers, record their actual responses and revise the treatment or shot plan.
minimum: Identify the creative assumption being tested.
Combine the planned image, timing and sound approach.
Record two responses and a concrete planning change.
advanced-w1-4.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w2-0.title: Light for movement
advanced-w2-0.idea: A lighting setup that works for a still subject may fail as they move. Walk through the action and examine exposure, direction, reflections and focus at each mark. Motivated sources can create a coherent space while controlled fill keeps essential detail readable. Do not assume one exposure value works everywhere. Rehearse and simplify the blocking if a safe, repeatable setup is not achievable.
advanced-w2-0.example: A person walking away from a window may lose facial detail. Changing their stopping mark can solve more than adding another light.
steps: Plan a subject moving through three marks. Test light and exposure at each position, then revise one source, reflector or movement. Document the change.
minimum: Show or storyboard exposure and shadow behaviour at three marks.
Explain why the apparent sources belong in the scene.
Document one change that improves repeatability.
advanced-w2-0.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w2-1.title: Match multiple cameras
advanced-w2-1.idea: Multiple cameras need more than matching resolution. Compare frame rate, shutter, white balance, picture profile and exposure with a shared reference. Cameras may render colour differently even with identical numbers. Record a sync cue and test long-take drift. If using one camera, repeated coverage can teach matching, but label it as repeated action rather than a simultaneous event.
advanced-w2-1.example: Two phones may use different automatic tone mapping. A neutral reference and actual edit test matter more than assuming identical settings guarantee a match.
steps: Capture two angles with matching settings or repeated one-camera takes. Record a sync cue, neutral reference and settings sheet. Match the shots in a short test edit.
minimum: Record the relevant settings and reference for both angles.
Show a sync method and check the start and end of the take.
Identify and correct an image mismatch.
advanced-w2-1.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w2-2.title: Record sound in layers
advanced-w2-2.idea: Dialogue, ambience and specific effects serve different storytelling roles. Capture clean sources and useful variations so the edit can shape perspective. Record a sound log with scene, take and any problem. Do not replace documentary sound in a way that misleads about what happened. For fiction, intentional sound design can suggest off-screen space while remaining clearly part of the constructed scene.
advanced-w2-2.example: A workshop can be established by room tone, a drawer, a tool and a small mechanism, without putting all sounds at the same volume.
steps: Record a short dialogue or action scene plus five separate sound elements and room tone. Log each source, distance and intended use. Make a rough sound-only sequence.
minimum: Explain how essential sound was isolated or protected.
Identify each recorded layer and any limitations.
Build a sound sequence that communicates a place or action.
advanced-w2-2.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w2-3.title: Keep a continuity record
advanced-w2-3.idea: Continuity includes action, costume, props, light, sound and the state of the story. Record the details that affect editing rather than trying to document everything equally. A take log should distinguish technical faults from performance preferences. Back up captured media before reformatting a card, and verify copies rather than relying on a folder icon. Keep originals separate from working edits.
advanced-w2-3.example: A cup changing hands can distract at a cut. A motivated cutaway may help, but the log should still identify the difference.
steps: Shoot a six-shot scene with a continuity sheet, take log and backup record. Deliberately compare two takes with one continuity difference and choose how to handle it.
minimum: Track the action and prop details that affect the cut.
Explain why the selected takes serve performance and clarity.
Record how the copied files were checked before reuse of media.
advanced-w2-3.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w2-4.title: Production study
advanced-w2-4.idea: A production study tests whether the planned system survives a real scene. Review image, sound and continuity together and identify the most expensive failure to repeat. Create a short assembly using your strongest takes, then name the missing coverage or repair you would prioritise. A useful debrief produces a change to the next shoot, not only a list of complaints.
advanced-w2-4.example: A missing reaction may matter more than a slightly noisy background. The debrief should rank fixes by their effect on the viewer.
steps: Assemble a 60–90 second scene with multi-angle coverage and layered sound. Include continuity records, a technical comparison and a one-page production debrief.
minimum: Show a clear action across multiple views.
Provide evidence of image matching, sound and continuity decisions.
Identify the highest-priority production improvement and why.
advanced-w2-4.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w3-0.title: Manage colour deliberately
advanced-w3-0.idea: A colour-managed workflow interprets source media and transforms it for the intended display. Input, working and output spaces are different decisions. Incorrect tagging or applying a transform twice can create misleading contrast and saturation. Test a short representative sequence first and use the official guidance for your software version. A display you have not calibrated limits how confidently you can judge delivery colour.
advanced-w3-0.example: A log image can look flat before a transform. Applying two transforms can crush shadows rather than create a richer grade.
steps: Document source, timeline and output colour handling for three clips. Compare the correct setup with a labelled incorrect transform, then record how you diagnosed the difference.
minimum: Identify the input and output assumptions for each clip.
Show or describe the effect of one incorrect transform.
Record the limits of the display and viewing setup used.
advanced-w3-0.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w3-1.title: Refine the image
advanced-w3-1.idea: Secondary corrections target a portion of the image. Qualifiers, windows and tracking need inspection through the entire shot; a clean still can hide flicker or a drifting mask. Use small corrections to direct attention while preserving believable texture and colour. Compare at normal playback speed and bypass the correction regularly. If the fix is more distracting than the problem, simplify it.
advanced-w3-1.example: A subtle lift on a face can help, but a bright oval that drifts away from it is worse than leaving the shot alone.
steps: Correct one distracting area with a window or equivalent local adjustment. Inspect the start, middle and end, compare with bypass and save evidence of one refinement.
minimum: Identify the distraction and the intended correction.
Check the affected area at three moments and normal playback.
Explain why the final strength improves attention without an obvious artifact.
advanced-w3-1.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w3-2.title: Finish the sound
advanced-w3-2.idea: Sound finishing balances intelligibility, perspective and dynamics. Repair only what needs repair; aggressive noise reduction can damage speech. Use meters and listening together, then compare against the actual delivery requirements rather than a universal loudness number. Check transitions and silence as carefully as loud moments. Keep a version before processing so changes remain reversible.
advanced-w3-2.example: A little room sound can feel more natural than speech damaged by extreme cleanup. The better choice depends on intelligibility and the scene.
steps: Mix a 60-second sequence with speech, ambience and effects. Compare unprocessed and repaired audio, check meters against a documented destination requirement and listen on two devices.
minimum: Keep the essential message clear across the sequence.
Identify a repair and any audible trade-off.
Record the delivery target and observations from two playback systems.
advanced-w3-2.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w3-3.title: Build titles and versions
advanced-w3-3.idea: Graphics should explain or support the film. Hierarchy, duration, contrast and safe placement affect readability more than animation complexity. Versioning requires deliberate reframing and careful proofing of every language or caption track. Keep editable text and project versions so revisions do not require rebuilding the entire film. Check the actual export rather than assuming the timeline preview is enough.
advanced-w3-3.example: A tasteful lower third can still fail if a platform overlay covers the name. The export must be tested in its intended viewing context.
steps: Create an opening title, a lower third and captions for two formats. Check contrast, reading time and safe placement. Export both and log any corrections.
minimum: Make the essential text readable at the intended screen size.
Reposition graphics deliberately for each format.
Proofread names, captions and timing in both exported files.
advanced-w3-3.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w3-4.title: Quality-control pass
advanced-w3-4.idea: A quality-control pass separates creative approval from technical delivery. Check the whole export for dropped or black frames, offline media, caption errors, unexpected levels and inconsistent colour. Use a checklist and record the file version inspected. Keep masters, viewing versions, project files and source media in a recoverable structure. A portfolio copy is not a substitute for an archive.
advanced-w3-4.example: A caption typo present in all three exports becomes easy to miss if you only inspect the timeline before rendering.
steps: Deliver a master and two viewing versions with captions where relevant. Complete a timed QC log, fix one issue or document a clean pass, then reopen the archived project.
minimum: Record an end-to-end check of the actual exported files.
Identify versions, settings and caption status clearly.
Demonstrate that the saved project and required media reopen.
advanced-w3-4.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w4-0.title: Scope your final film
advanced-w4-0.idea: A portfolio project should demonstrate a clear strength and a complete process. Keep its scope achievable with the people, access and time you have. Specify the audience and the craft decisions you want to prove. Use a short treatment and schedule that another person could understand. If working alone, simplify the production rather than pretending to have a crew or equipment you do not have.
advanced-w4-0.example: A precise portrait of one maker can demonstrate more control than a broad film about an entire industry that you cannot access.
steps: Choose a product, documentary, travel, social or fictional film brief. Write the treatment, deliverables, schedule and three craft goals. Identify the biggest risk and a smaller fallback film.
minimum: Define one audience, purpose and 2–3 minute deliverable.
Name three craft choices the finished film should demonstrate.
Provide a realistic schedule and smaller fallback.
advanced-w4-0.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w4-1.title: Shoot the essentials
advanced-w4-1.idea: Protect the shots and sounds the film cannot work without. Check them on location while another take is still possible. Use a take log, consent records and verified backups. If the story changes during filming, update the brief honestly instead of forcing the footage into an unsupported claim. Record the gap between the original plan and what was actually captured.
advanced-w4-1.example: A missing final action can change the ending. Recognising it during the shoot is more useful than discovering it after the location closes.
steps: Shoot or build a labelled storyboard version of the essential sequence. Save a six-frame contact sheet, sound plan, take log and backup record. Identify any missing beat before editing.
minimum: Account for every essential story beat.
Record image, sound, permission and backup checks.
Distinguish captured evidence from planned or simulated material.
advanced-w4-1.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w4-2.title: Make a review cut
advanced-w4-2.idea: A review cut should be understandable without your explanation. Ask viewers what they noticed, where attention dropped and what they believe the film says. Record disagreement and confusion as useful evidence. Separate a response to the story from a request for a favourite effect. Keep the version you tested so the final revision can be compared against it.
advanced-w4-2.example: “What did you think the maker cared about?” reveals more than “Did you like my cinematic shots?”
steps: Create a complete rough cut. Show it to two viewers, collect three neutral observations from each and sort changes by story clarity, image, sound and delivery.
minimum: Show an opening, development and ending.
Record two viewers’ actual responses without leading them.
Rank changes by their effect on the brief.
advanced-w4-2.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w4-3.title: Refine and deliver
advanced-w4-3.idea: The final pass should address the most important evidence from the review. Recheck the entire film after each major change because fixing one cut can disturb sound, captions or timing elsewhere. Deliver the agreed versions, then verify playback outside the editing application. Record unresolved limitations plainly; a credible case study describes judgment rather than pretending the result is flawless.
advanced-w4-3.example: If a shorter opening clarifies the film, check that the new first shot still has enough context and that the audio starts cleanly.
steps: Finish the 2–3 minute film and one short-format version. Complete picture, sound, caption, permission and export checks. Compare one major revision with the review cut.
minimum: Explain one major revision using viewer or technical evidence.
Check image, sound, text and permissions across the finished film.
Play the exported versions end to end and record their settings.
advanced-w4-3.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

advanced-w4-4.title: Publish your case study
advanced-w4-4.idea: A case study helps someone understand your contribution and decisions. Show the brief, a few purposeful frames, one comparison and the finished work. Credit collaborators and state whether exercises were simulated. Share only material you have permission to publish. Choose the next learning priority from repeated weaknesses across the project, not merely the newest piece of equipment.
advanced-w4-4.example: A strong case study can explain why a simpler lighting setup served the subject and what the first version taught you.
steps: Save the final film or viewing link with a concise case study: brief, your role, three decisions, before/after evidence, feedback and next practice goal. Add it to My work and share only if you choose.
minimum: State your role and credit other contributors.
Support three decisions with frames, notes or comparisons.
Check sharing permission and name a specific next practice goal.
advanced-w4-4.alternative: Use your own stills, a labelled storyboard, a settings comparison or a paper edit if equipment or filming access is unavailable. Show the planned decisions and likely trade-offs. Clearly label a simulation; do not claim that unseen footage or unrecorded sound was tested.

new:consent-privacy.title: Decide what can be recorded and shared
new:consent-privacy.idea: Permission to record and permission to share are separate decisions. Agree the purpose, audience and boundaries before a camera is running. A person should be able to decline without pressure. Avoid identifying details you do not need: addresses, documents, screens, uniforms and location clues can identify someone even without a face. For children, seek the responsible adult’s permission and the child’s willing participation; use objects or adult stand-ins for this pilot. Venue permission does not automatically cover everyone at an event.
new:consent-privacy.example: A maker agrees to a private training clip, but not an advertisement. The same footage cannot simply move from the training folder to a public reel.
steps: Use fictional names to write what will be recorded, why, who may see it and what must stay out.
Choose a safe stand-in and check the background for identifiers. Use only your own or properly licensed music; save the licence conditions.
Decide where originals will be kept, when access ends and who to contact if sharing permission changes.
minimum: Use fictional names to write what will be recorded, why, who may see it and what must stay out.
Choose a safe stand-in and check the background for identifiers. Use only your own or properly licensed music; save the licence conditions.
Decide where originals will be kept, when access ends and who to contact if sharing permission changes.

new:memory-capture.title: Save the moment and find it again
new:memory-capture.idea: A useful memory does not need many cuts. Keep the recognisable person, action or sound, leave a little time before and after the moment, and test playback before putting the phone away. Keep the original private until everyone affected is comfortable with sharing. A descriptive note and a second copy make the moment useful later.
new:memory-capture.example: A close-up of a birthday candle preserves a detail; a steady view including the greeting preserves the moment. A private filename such as “October greeting—original” makes it findable without exposing a full address.
steps: Choose an ordinary safe moment and name what must be recognisable.
Record a short steady take with the important sound, or plan it with an object stand-in.
Replay it, add a meaningful note and find the copy again from a different folder.
minimum: The subject and moment can be identified without an explanation.
The important action is in frame and any necessary words are understandable.
The original has a meaningful name or note and is retrievable by the intended private viewer.

new:evidence-capture.title: Record context without altering the record
new:evidence-capture.idea: Start with context, then show the detail. Keep identity, location within the scene and the observed condition connected; do not fill gaps with a reconstruction. A factual note separates what you saw from what you believe caused it. Preserve the device original, timestamps and relevant surrounding footage. Make separately labelled viewing or redacted copies; do not overwrite the original. This is filming practice, not advice about legal admissibility.
new:evidence-capture.example: For a damaged mug, a wide view establishes the whole object before the camera moves to a crack. A dramatic montage of the crack cannot establish that context by itself.
steps: Use a harmless owned object, not a real dispute or private document. Record an overview, identifying feature and detail in a connected take.
Log capture time, device, what is visible and what remains uncertain. Do not claim the camera proves a cause.
Keep the unmodified original and a separate named viewing copy. Check that a recipient can relate the detail to the whole.
minimum: A wide context view links the identifying detail and observed condition without a gap that changes meaning.
Important marks are readable; relevant sounds are retained without enhancement presented as original.
The unmodified original and a factual capture/context log remain linked; sharing copies are labelled.

new:process-steps.title: Show every necessary step
new:process-steps.idea: A demonstration works when the viewer can repeat the necessary actions. Identify the starting state, each action that changes it, and the visible result. Let the critical action finish in frame; a beautiful close-up is unhelpful if it hides where the tool goes. Separate normal steps from optional variations. Use safe everyday processes, not unqualified medical, electrical or hazardous instruction.
new:process-steps.example: For folding a paper envelope, showing the fold line and hand movement is more useful than a fast montage of finished envelopes.
steps: List three to five steps of a safe process, including the starting materials.
Film a short sample with an unobstructed view and a pause at each state change.
Ask a viewer which step is missing or unclear; revise that step and keep a numbered text alternative.
minimum: All critical steps and their order are visible or explicitly described.
Hands tools and results can be distinguished, with quantities or orientation where needed.
A viewer can repeat the approved process or identify the point needing qualified help.

new:motion-analysis.title: Compare movement consistently
new:motion-analysis.idea: Useful comparison needs a stable viewpoint and the full relevant movement. Keep camera height, distance, frame rate and framing consistent; record the conditions so differences are not mistaken for changes in performance. Slow playback can help observation but does not create missing frames or validate a measurement. Separate visible observations from coaching, diagnosis or claims about injury.
new:motion-analysis.example: If one throw is filmed from the side and another from the front, apparent differences may come from the camera. A fixed wide view lets a qualified coach interpret the movement in context.
steps: Record two harmless movements from one stable position with permission. Keep the relevant body or object in frame.
Log viewpoint, capture frame rate and start/end timestamps. Compare equivalent moments at normal and slower playback.
Write only observations, then name what a qualified coach or clinician would need to interpret.
minimum: The relevant movement remains visible from a stable angle with known playback speed.
Compared attempts use a consistent viewpoint, framing and timing reference.
Observations are separated from diagnoses; only the authorised learner or reviewer receives the sample.

new:event-backup.title: Rehearse the moment you cannot repeat
new:event-backup.idea: An event may not happen twice. Identify the essential moment, a dependable recording position and the sound you cannot lose. Test batteries, storage and playback before the event, and name a backup for power, audio and recording. A checklist is only useful if you rehearse what happens when one item fails. A staged exercise is not proof of readiness to cover a paid wedding alone.
new:event-backup.example: A beautiful roaming shot does not replace a continuous view of the vows. Protect a stable primary recording before collecting decorative detail.
steps: Stage a 60-second announcement with a consenting adult or recorded stand-in.
Run a sound and storage check, record the essential moment, and practise switching to a backup.
Replay the complete take and log any gap. For a real event, arrange supervision and agree the coverage and permissions.
minimum: One agreed essential segment is complete with enough context to identify the participants.
Speech is understandable and critical action is not obscured or lost between angles.
Permission, a checked backup and the promised delivery format are documented.

new:interview-care.title: Ask listen and represent fairly
new:interview-care.idea: An interview begins with listening. Agree the topic, recording choice and intended audience, then ask an open question and allow time for an answer. Ask for clarification without suggesting the answer you want. In the edit, preserve the speaker’s meaning and relevant context; do not join unrelated words to imply something they did not say. Sensitive testimony needs appropriate safeguarding and qualified support.
new:interview-care.example: “Tell me how you learned this skill” invites an account. “You found it easy, didn’t you?” supplies the account for the speaker.
steps: Use a consenting adult volunteer for a harmless topic, or write both sides as a labelled simulation.
Ask one open question, record a clean answer and note the consent boundaries.
Make a short excerpt or transcript, compare it with the full answer and flag anything that could change the meaning.
minimum: An open question and intact answer convey the speaker’s meaning without a leading edit.
Essential words can be understood and the speaker stays in usable focus.
Recording and sharing choices are agreed, with accurate name/context and a restricted original.

new:creative-brief.title: Make one visual idea work
new:creative-brief.idea: A creative brief names a viewer, a change and a constraint. Choose one feeling or idea that a small sequence can communicate. The order and duration of shots affect what the viewer expects; test those choices before adding effects. Fiction may construct events, but participants still need agreed roles, safe working conditions and clear sharing permission.
new:creative-brief.example: The same door opening can suggest anticipation or relief. The preceding shot and the pause before it matter as much as the door itself.
steps: Write one intended feeling and a beginning, change and ending for an ordinary safe action.
Storyboard two orders, then capture or assemble the smaller version.
Show it without explaining the intention, record the response and adjust one decision.
minimum: A viewer can identify the intended change or feeling in the sequence.
Image, sound and timing choices consistently support that intention.
A before/after revision and rights-cleared playable delivery are shown.

new:place-observation.title: Observe a place respectfully
new:place-observation.idea: A place becomes understandable through relationships: an establishing view locates the viewer, an action shows how it is used, and a detail makes it specific. Work from safe permitted positions without disturbing people, wildlife or restricted spaces. Avoid extreme wide-angle views that misrepresent room proportions in commercial property work. Distinguish an observed fact from a feeling or claim.
new:place-observation.example: A property walkthrough should connect the entrance, room and exit so a viewer understands the layout. Isolated attractive corners cannot show the relationship between rooms.
steps: Choose a safe accessible place and define what the viewer needs to understand.
Make an overview, a connecting movement or route, and a distinctive detail. Keep people and private identifiers out unless agreed.
Ask a viewer to describe the layout or place from the sample; fill one missing connection.
minimum: A wide view and specific details let an unfamiliar viewer locate the subject.
The place and relevant natural sound are legible without invented context.
Access, non-disturbance and any sensitive location omissions are explained.

new:creator-brief.title: Make one promise to one viewer
new:creator-brief.idea: An opening makes a promise. Keep it specific enough that the rest of the video can deliver it. Demonstrate the useful action before repeating it in text; captions should retain meaning when sound is off. Avoid misleading before-and-after edits or a claim you cannot support. Match the destination’s frame shape deliberately and check text on a real phone.
new:creator-brief.example: “Three ways to keep herbs fresh” needs three demonstrated methods. A dramatic opening that never shows the method loses the viewer’s trust.
steps: Choose one viewer and one useful takeaway that you can demonstrate safely.
Make a short opening, proof and payoff using your own footage.
Check the sample without sound and revise captions or framing where the meaning disappears.
minimum: The opening establishes what this viewer will get from the piece.
The sequence communicates one idea without an unexplained gap or redundant section.
Captions and framing survive a phone check and all included media has a documented basis for use.

new:commercial-claims.title: Show the benefit truthfully
new:commercial-claims.idea: A benefit is useful only when the evidence supports it. Write the exact claim, the action that demonstrates it and any limitation a viewer needs to know. Keep conditions comparable in a before-and-after demonstration. Credit licensed assets and disclose relevant sponsorship or relationships according to the destination’s requirements. Get specialist review for regulated claims.
new:commercial-claims.example: A bag shown holding a laptop demonstrates fit. It does not establish that the bag is waterproof or safe for every device.
steps: Choose an owned product or a fictional campaign. List one claim and what would visibly support it.
Record the product in normal use with readable context; avoid implying a result you did not test.
Review wording, permissions and the next action with a viewer; remove an unsupported claim.
checks: Disclosures access and useful call to action
minimum: A visible demonstration supports the stated benefit without an unsupported promise.
The relevant features or actions remain visible and the explanation understandable.
Necessary disclosures, readable text and an accurate next action survive the target-device check.

new:teaching-chunks.title: Teach one objective at a time
new:teaching-chunks.idea: A lesson should help the learner do one thing. State the objective as an observable action, show a worked example and leave a pause to try it. Break long explanations at decision points. Speak the essential visual information and supply a concise text version; captions need correction rather than blind acceptance of automatic output. Use fictional learner details and avoid exposing class records.
new:teaching-chunks.example: A lesson about fractions can ask the learner to divide one paper shape, show the action, then pause. Ten minutes of definitions may never reveal whether the learner can do it.
steps: Write one learning objective and a three-step example using harmless materials.
Record a two- to five-minute sample, with readable framing and a deliberate practice pause.
Ask a learner or adult stand-in to perform the action; revise a confusing step and supply a short transcript.
minimum: One learning objective is demonstrated accurately in complete ordered steps.
The intended learner can see and hear or read the essential explanation.
A checked transcript/caption alternative and one learner task test the intended objective.

new:screen-capture.title: Record a readable private screen
new:screen-capture.idea: Record the smallest screen area that explains the action. Close personal tabs, hide notifications and use dummy accounts or data. Check text size at the viewer’s device size, slow down at the important click and narrate changes that are not visually obvious. Recording a call requires a separate permission decision; a private connection test need not be recorded.
new:screen-capture.example: A bug report needs the starting state, steps and actual result. Recording the entire desktop can expose messages without adding useful evidence.
steps: Prepare a dummy screen and a short list of actions; hide notifications and unrelated windows.
Capture one window or phone screen with an understandable pointer and narration or equivalent text.
Play it back at phone size, check for exposed data and note the expected versus actual result.
minimum: The intended screen action or message is readable at the receiver’s viewing size.
Speech or equivalent text explains the action without a missing transition.
Private data is absent and the file or live connection works for the intended recipient.

new:live-rehearsal.title: Test the stream and its fallback
new:live-rehearsal.idea: A stream is a chain: source, sound, encoder, connection and receiver. A clean preview on the sending computer does not prove that the audience is receiving clear sound and picture. Test privately at the receiver, allow for delay and keep a local recording when permitted. Decide what viewers should see if the connection fails. A course score does not certify a broadcast or emergency communication system.
new:live-rehearsal.example: The presenter’s headphones sound fine, but the stream is receiving the laptop microphone. A receiver check catches the wrong audio source before the event.
steps: Run a private rehearsal with fictional content on the equipment and connection you will use.
Inspect picture, sound and sync from a receiver, then deliberately stop the test uplink.
Try the fallback message, verify the local recording and log the recovery. If no stable uplink is available, practise locally and label streaming untested.
minimum: A private rehearsal survives a planned failure or switches to the stated fallback.
Programme speech is understandable and sync is checked at the receiving end.
Rights, access alternative and moderation/stop responsibility are assigned.

new:report-verification.title: Keep facts sources and safety together
new:report-verification.idea: A report separates observations, attributed accounts and uncertainty. Record what the camera actually shows and keep the origin and time context linked to the original. Do not use a reconstruction as if it were eyewitness footage. Protect sources and bystanders before publishing; anonymity may require more than blurring a face. This pilot uses fictional harmless incidents and does not provide legal or investigative advice.
new:report-verification.example: A puddle in a corridor shows water on a floor. It does not prove who caused it or when the leak began. An account from a witness needs attribution and checking.
steps: Stage a harmless fictional event and record context plus detail.
Write three columns: observed, reported by someone, and not yet verified.
Make a short factual summary, label any reconstruction and identify details that should remain private.
minimum: Who, what, when and where are recorded with sources and uncertainty identified.
A sequence does not reverse chronology or imply an unsupported causal claim.
A documented source-risk decision and linked unmodified originals control what can be shared.

new:technical-log.title: Make an observation repeatable
new:technical-log.idea: A technical recording is useful when another person can understand its setup and limits. Record scale, viewpoint, lighting, frame timing and any calibration assumptions. A compressed clip or a pleasing reconstruction may conceal uncertainty. Use approved protocols and qualified supervision for real industrial, scientific or clinical work; rehearse here with safe tabletop objects.
new:technical-log.example: A toy rolling past a marked ruler can demonstrate a logging method. It cannot validate a crash-test camera system or justify measurements from unknown frame timing.
steps: Set up a harmless tabletop proxy with a visible reference and a fixed viewpoint.
Capture a short sample and log device, scale, timing and environmental conditions.
Repeat once, describe what changed and state which measurements or conclusions the recording cannot support.
minimum: The procedure, viewpoint, scale and timing needed to interpret the observation are recorded.
The relevant event is visible at a stated real or playback rate without hidden manipulation.
An approved safe method and identifiable unmodified source files accompany the record.

new:archive-preservation.title: Keep originals context and access copies
new:archive-preservation.idea: An archive keeps files, context and access decisions together. Preserve originals separately from edits, use a consistent naming scheme and verify a copy by opening it or checking integrity with an appropriate tool. Keep another copy in a separate location when possible. Old tapes and obsolete formats need compatible playback or a qualified digitisation service; do not discard the source after one unverified transfer.
new:archive-preservation.example: “final-final2.mp4” says little. A manifest connecting the original, date, creator, permission and access copy explains what the file is and how it may be used.
steps: Use an owned sample and write a manifest: identifier, source, date, description, permission and versions.
Make a separate copy and test retrieval and playback; label any restoration as an edit.
Ask a safe stand-in recipient to find the requested item from the manifest, then fix one ambiguity.
minimum: An unmodified source and any restoration or access-copy changes are identified.
A catalogue entry locates the source and a checked playable copy.
Access wishes and at least one separate verified copy or preservation handoff are documented.

new:aerial-safety.title: Prepare an authorised aerial plan
new:aerial-safety.idea: Plan the shot from the ground before considering a flight. Identify the purpose, location, nearby people and airspace constraints. Actual flight depends on current Indian DGCA and airspace requirements, permissions, equipment and operator competence. Check the official portal for the specific place and date; an old tutorial or green area on a screenshot is not a flight authorisation. Do not practise near people, airports or other hazards to complete a lesson.
new:aerial-safety.example: A ground storyboard can explain the intended reveal without launching a drone. It teaches shot purpose while flight planning remains a separate qualified decision.
steps: Create a ground-based shot map and a no-flight alternative.
List the current official checks, site permission and operator requirements that remain to be confirmed.
Review the plan with a qualified operator. Only label real aerial capture complete after the actual authorised work and evidence exist.
minimum: The learner documents the current permission/airspace checks and a safe authorised plan or labels a ground rehearsal.
The aerial or simulated view answers the location brief without unsafe approach or misleading orientation.
Incidental privacy, file context and the receiving format are checked.

new:spatial-spec.title: Match the geometry and target device
new:spatial-spec.idea: Spatial media depends on its target pipeline. A 360 viewing experience, an object reconstruction and a projection loop need different capture and delivery choices. Confirm geometry, resolution, stitching or overlap, audio and the viewing device before capture. Keep motion comfortable and check seams or alignment. A flat storyboard can plan the experience but cannot prove a headset, reconstruction or installation works.
new:spatial-spec.example: A reframe extracted from 360 footage becomes a flat video. It is different from delivering a navigable spherical file with the metadata required by a 360 player.
steps: Name the target device or receiving pipeline and its required format.
Use compatible equipment or a clearly labelled storyboard to test viewpoints, overlap or alignment on a harmless subject.
Check the sample in the actual target system or record what is still untested. Seek a qualified operator for installations or validated measurement.
minimum: The specified geometry, coverage or overlap is demonstrated on a test asset.
A target-viewer test checks seams, motion comfort, legibility or display alignment as applicable.
The exported test follows the actual device specification and documents privacy limits.

new:temporal-capture.title: Control change between frames
new:temporal-capture.idea: Stop motion and time-lapse turn separate images into apparent movement. Stability, consistent light and controlled changes between frames matter more than effects. Output duration equals the number of frames divided by playback frames per second. Capture interval controls how much real-world time a time-lapse represents; it is different from playback rate. Preserve the source frames and label speed changes.
new:temporal-capture.example: Twenty-four pictures played at 12 fps last two seconds. Moving an object by a smaller equal step between pictures creates a different motion than changing the export label alone.
steps: Fix a phone or camera safely and use one small owned object under steady light.
Capture a short sequence with a frame count and a note of each change. Avoid touching the camera between frames.
Compare playback at two rates, identify flicker or uneven spacing and repeat a short section with one improvement.
minimum: The change across frames is intentional and has a clear start and end.
Position, light and frame timing remain consistent or the deliberate change is logged.
Playback speed is stated and source frames or settings make the method repeatable.

new:accessible-communication.title: Keep the meaning accessible
new:accessible-communication.idea: Accessibility is part of the message. Identify which information is only heard, only seen or dependent on timing. Provide accurate captions for speech and meaningful sounds, and a description or descriptive transcript for essential visual information. Sign-language communication needs a competent signer, appropriate framing and language review; automatic captions do not replace sign language. Ask intended users what they need without treating one person as representative of everyone.
new:accessible-communication.example: “Put it there” depends on seeing a pointing hand. “Place the cup on the left shelf” carries the instruction in words as well as the image.
steps: Choose a short harmless message and list information lost with sound off or eyes away.
Create a captioned sample and a descriptive text alternative, or plan a signed version with a qualified signer.
Check timing, names, placement and meaning with an appropriate reviewer; label any unreviewed language or access requirement.
minimum: The essential spoken and visual meaning has an appropriate equivalent for the stated access need.
Captions, description or signing are complete, legible and correctly timed.
A competent speaker/sign user or intended viewer checks meaning on the delivery device.

new:delivery-originals.title: Check the file and keep the original
new:delivery-originals.idea: Delivery begins with the recipient’s actual need. Confirm file shape, length, sound, captions and access method before export. Test the exported file outside the editor and on the intended device. Keep originals separate from viewing copies, and mark transformations such as redaction, reframing or time changes. For a private call, test the connection without creating a recording by default.
new:delivery-originals.example: A vertical preview can look fine in an editor while captions are clipped on the phone. A factual original can lose context if it is cropped just to fit a feed.
steps: Check the requested format and decide which transformations are appropriate for this task.
Open the actual output or test connection on the receiving device; check beginning, middle and end, sound and text.
Name originals and access copies clearly, set appropriate sharing permissions and record the result of the check.
minimum: Check the requested format and decide which transformations are appropriate for this task.
Open the actual output or test connection on the receiving device; check beginning, middle and end, sound and text.
Name originals and access copies clearly, set appropriate sharing permissions and record the result of the check.

new:reflect-revise.title: Compare improve and explain
new:reflect-revise.idea: A useful score points to evidence and a next action. Compare the work with the criteria, name the weakest part and change one thing. Keep the earlier version so the comparison is real. A self-check reports your judgement; AI sees only your text and a selected still, not motion or sound. Neither can certify legal, clinical, flight or professional readiness. Record any qualified review still needed separately from completing the exercise.
new:reflect-revise.example: “The sound is good” is a claim. A listening log can describe what you heard and where you changed microphone position, but an AI that has not heard the recording still cannot verify the result.
steps: Use the score anchors to identify what your evidence actually demonstrates.
Make one short revision, keep the previous version and explain the difference.
Log what is still untested, who should review it and the next practical step.
minimum: Use the score anchors to identify what your evidence actually demonstrates.
Make one short revision, keep the previous version and explain the difference.
Log what is still untested, who should review it and the next practical step.
